blocks.text: Paul anchors Timothy's calling in his family history of faith. The letter names two women—his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice—as exemplars of genuine, lived faith. Paul grounds his exhortation to Timothy by appealing to this maternal lineage and his own memory of Timothy's sincere faith, suggesting that Timothy's commitment stands in continuity with his family's spiritual heritage.

Paul reminds Timothy to kindle or stir up the divine gift within him—a gift identified as imparted through the laying on of the sender's hands. This ritual act of hand-laying connected the gift to authorization and commission. The exhortation to rekindle it suggests either that the gift had dimmed through disuse or that Timothy needed encouragement to activate it fully. Paul immediately assures that the spirit God imparts is one of power, love, and self-discipline.

The letter's central exhortation calls Timothy not to be ashamed—of the gospel's testimony, of Paul himself (now imprisoned), or of his own commitment to Christ. Instead, Timothy is urged to share willingly in hardship for the sake of the gospel, trusting in God's power and grace. This framing presents Christian witness as costly but as empowered by divine resource rather than human strength alone. The call moves beyond mere acknowledgment to active, costly solidarity with the gospel message.

The chapter closes by noting defection among those in Asia who had turned away from Paul, naming Phygelus and Hermogenes as examples. In stark contrast stands Onesiphorus, praised for his refreshment of Paul, his refusal to be ashamed of Paul's imprisonment, his diligent search for Paul, and his prior faithful service at Ephesus. Onesiphorus embodies the costly loyalty and unashamed witness that the letter has been calling Timothy to embrace—making him a living counterexample to desertion.
